# A map of the bacteria

> *Lectures name bacteria by group: Gram-positive cocci, Enterobacterales, anaerobes, atypicals. Each
> group shares a few traits, and from those traits we can read how its members live.*

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Learning objectives
- Describe a bacterial group by its envelope, shape, oxygen use, growth in the laboratory and where it
  grows relative to host cells.
- Distinguish extracellular, facultative intracellular and obligate intracellular bacteria.
- Explain how what a bacterium needs predicts where it lives and how it spreads.
- Explain why the atypical bacteria escape routine stains and culture, and what follows for their
  detection and treatment.
- Name the group a bacterium belongs to from a few of its traits.
:::

## Reading a group as a set of traits {#sec-map-idea}

A bacterium is described by five traits: envelope, shape, additional structures, oxygen and growth
rate (see [*How bacteria are built and get
energy*](../principles/bacteria-build-energy.qmd#sec-bact-toolkit)). Groups also differ in what they
need in the laboratory: ordinary media, enriched media, weeks of incubation, or living cells. A
bacterial group can be described in those terms.

::: {.example}
Enterobacterales are Gram-negative rods that grow with or without oxygen, ferment sugars, and live in
the gut.
:::

### Where bacteria grow {#sec-map-where}

Whole groups differ in where they grow relative to host cells. **Extracellular** bacteria grow
outside host cells, **facultative intracellular** bacteria grow inside or outside them, and **obligate
intracellular** bacteria grow only inside them.

::: {.spectrum}
[Where bacteria grow relative to host cells]{.tree-title}

- Extracellular: outside cells, such as Enterobacterales
- Facultative intracellular: inside or outside cells, such as mycobacteria
- Obligate intracellular: only inside cells, such as *Chlamydia*

[Independent of host cells]{.spectrum-end} [Dependent on host cells]{.spectrum-end}
:::

The more a group depends on host cells, the more the laboratory has to supply: an obligate
intracellular bacterium grows only in a culture of living cells.

### Where group names come from {#sec-map-names}

Group names come from three different sources.

::: {.concept-tree}
[Sources of group names]{.tree-title}

- Taxonomy
  - Enterobacterales, an order
  - Mycobacteria, the genus *Mycobacterium*
- Traits
  - One trait: anaerobes (oxygen), spiral bacteria (shape)
  - Two traits: Gram-positive cocci, Gram-negative cocci (envelope and shape)
- Behaviour in the laboratory
  - Fastidious Gram-negatives, which need enriched media
  - Atypicals, which escape routine stains and culture
:::

Because the sources differ, the groups overlap: *Clostridium* is both a Gram-positive rod and an
anaerobe.

## What the traits predict {#sec-map-predict}

### Metabolism and needs predict habitat {#sec-map-habitat}

*Escherichia coli* and *Pseudomonas aeruginosa* are both Gram-negative rods, but the first lives in the
gut and the second in water and soil, largely because of how each makes ATP.

<div data-island="contrast-pair" data-src="/diagrams/pair-ecoli-pseudomonas.yml"></div>

A **fastidious** organism grows only when the laboratory meets special requirements. Often the reason
is lost biosynthesis: over evolutionary time, a bacterium living on a rich host can lose the genes for
making nutrients the host already supplies, and then depends on finding them.

::: {.example}
*Haemophilus* needs two factors found inside red blood cells, so the laboratory grows it on agar made
with blood heated until the cells lyse, which is **chocolate agar**, named for its brown colour.
:::

Fragility outside the host limits spread in a related way. A bacterium that lives only in humans and
dies quickly in air cannot travel through water, soil or surfaces, so it passes only by close contact.

::: {.example}
*Neisseria meningitidis* and *Neisseria gonorrhoeae*, the Gram-negative cocci that cause most disease,
dry out in air and need enriched media in the laboratory. *N. meningitidis* spreads through
respiratory secretions and *N. gonorrhoeae* by sexual contact.
:::

### Why "atypical"? {#sec-map-atypicals}

In this course, the **atypical** bacteria are three genera, *Mycoplasma*, *Chlamydia* and
*Rickettsia*, from different branches of the bacterial tree, grouped because routine stains and
culture fail on them. Clinicians use the related term "atypical pneumonia" for an overlapping list of
causes that includes *Mycoplasma pneumoniae*, *Chlamydia pneumoniae* and *Legionella*.

Routine methods fail for two reasons: *Mycoplasma* has no wall, and *Chlamydia* and *Rickettsia* grow
only inside host cells. Each reason predicts how the organism is detected and which drugs can reach
it.

| | *Mycoplasma* | *Chlamydia* | *Rickettsia* |
|---|---|---|---|
| What is unusual | No cell wall at all | Obligate intracellular; two-form life cycle | Obligate intracellular, free in the cytoplasm |
| Envelope | Membrane only, stiffened with sterols | Gram-negative type, with very little peptidoglycan | Gram-negative type |
| Energy | Makes its own ATP | Takes ATP from the host cell as well as making some of its own | Takes ATP from the host cell as well as making its own |
| Transmission | Respiratory particles | Sexual or eye-to-eye contact, or respiratory particles, depending on the species | Arthropod vectors: ticks, lice, fleas or mites |
| Gram stain | No wall, so no Gram reaction | Too small, and hidden inside cells | Stains poorly |
| Laboratory growth | Slowly, on media enriched with sterols | Only in living cells | Only in living cells |

Starting from the missing wall, we can predict the other traits of *M. pneumoniae*.

<div data-island="microbe-profile" data-src="/diagrams/profile-m-pneumoniae.yml"></div>

*Chlamydia* also fails the Gram stain and will not grow on agar, but for a different reason.

<div data-island="contrast-pair" data-src="/diagrams/pair-mycoplasma-chlamydia.yml"></div>

::: {.callout-important}
## A common idea, corrected: "atypical means rare or unimportant"
"Atypical" refers to how these bacteria behave in the laboratory and the clinic, not to how often
they cause disease. *Chlamydia trachomatis* is one of the most common sexually transmitted bacteria in
the world, and *M. pneumoniae* is a common cause of pneumonia in children and young adults. Standard
stains and cultures miss them, so laboratories usually detect them by their nucleic acid.
:::

Much of how these infections are diagnosed and treated follows from the missing wall or the life
inside cells: drugs that act on the wall cannot treat *Mycoplasma*, and drugs for *Chlamydia* and
*Rickettsia* must enter host cells.

## Using the map {#sec-map-use}

### The group chapters {#sec-map-template}

Each group chapter covers one group from the map and has the same layout:

| Part of the chapter | Content |
|---|---|
| The group in one sentence | The group's row on the map, as a description |
| Sorting key | The few traits that separate members of the group, and what each trait means |
| Main organisms | Two or three organisms, each with a full profile card and its patterns of harm: how a mechanism leads to a kind of damage, with one example |
| Contrast pairs | The organisms most easily confused, side by side |
| Supporting organisms | One table row each |
| Later in the course | Where the organ-system blocks add diseases, diagnosis and treatment |
